# Continual-ARC demo budgeting

Use alongside `continual-arc-solving` and `arc-demo-validation` when deciding whether to request another demonstration.

## Workflow
1. Before a request, write down the leading candidate rule(s), the unresolved uncertainty, and how plausible incoming examples would distinguish the candidates. If the request has no clear discriminating purpose, do not spend it yet.
2. On receipt, compare the new input-output pair with the complete accumulated demo ledger, not only with the latest pair. Keep dimensions, color roles, object geometry, and changed cells exact.
3. After each pair, make forward progress: update the hypothesis, implement or revise the candidate transform, run it over all available pairs, and derive its test output when it passes. A demo request is not a substitute for executing these checks.
4. Reassess the expected value of another request against its fixed scoring cost and remaining budget. Stop requesting when evidence is sufficient to choose a validated rule, or when another example is unlikely to discriminate the remaining alternatives.
5. Never claim validation from visual plausibility or a partial match. Candidate eligibility still requires exact full-grid equality on every received demo.

## Pitfalls
- Repeatedly requesting examples without incorporating earlier ones wastes budget and leaves the task unsolved.
- A plausible object-level story is not a rule; state the selector and operation and check negative cases.
- Do not submit a manually assembled grid instead of the output generated by the validated task program.

## Related skills
`continual-arc-solving` defines the one-action protocol and per-task program lifecycle. `arc-demo-validation` defines exact fixture validation and hypothesis control. These overlap in demo acquisition guidance; consolidate there when curator policy permits.

# Session note: demo-request loop and unsupported submissions

In this instance, eight demos were requested consecutively without maintaining a runnable fixture ledger or testing a shared transform. Examples showed localized edits amid varied palettes/layouts, but no selector-operation model was built. After the cap, successive submissions tried arbitrary recolorings and identity, and each was rejected. This records a process failure, not a solved task rule.

After each demo, stop and integrate it: preserve exact input/output grids, diff every cell, note unchanged lookalikes, and run candidates against all accumulated fixtures. Request another pair only after naming competing hypotheses and a concrete discriminator. After a rejection, retire that rule family rather than trying palette substitutions or identity. With demos exhausted, only submit a materially distinct candidate grounded in all evidence; never call it verified without exact full-grid regression. Persist no speculative recurring-task program.

# Long-instance demo-request discipline

This instance illustrates a failure mode in extended Continual-ARC tasks: despite each demo carrying cost, repeated requests continued through most of the demo budget without an explicit accumulated hypothesis ledger, concrete discriminating question, implementation attempt, or verified test output. The incoming pairs varied widely in dimensions, palette, and local changes; repeated examples alone did not establish a common transform.

Reusable procedure:
- After each pair, capture exact dimensions and changed-cell coordinates/values, and state which existing hypothesis it supports or falsifies.
- Maintain named candidate selectors and operations, with negative examples that each candidate must explain.
- Before another request, specify which feature in a likely incoming pair would make the remaining candidates predict different outputs. If no such feature is named, do not request reflexively; synthesize the current evidence and assess whether any candidate passes every fixture.
- A final available demo is worthwhile only if an obtainable contrast can plausibly resolve the live ambiguity. Use all accumulated fixtures for exact validation; do not call a pattern verified based on visual impressions.
- When demos look structurally different, test a single abstract transformation across them (including only evidence-supported orientations) before treating them as separate task families.

This note records a process lesson, not a task-specific transform or solution.

# Separating palette mapping from target-color selection

When demos show a two-color recoloring, do not infer the selector solely from one example. A frequent hypothesis is that the majority/background color is changed into the minority/marker color while the minority cells become zero; a competing rule may instead select a fixed input color, or invert a global palette mapping. Compare exact frequencies and color identities across demos with different palettes and marker densities. Include degenerate or sparse examples, but recognize their limits: a single exceptional cell can establish how a marker is treated while leaving frequency-based selection ambiguous. Verify the proposed selector and operation over every complete pair, not merely the colors or a few cells.

A useful hypothesis ledger records for each demo: dimensions, palette, per-color counts, proposed selector, cell mapping, and exact equality status. If a new example contradicts the current density rule, retire it rather than silently changing mappings or hard-coding that palette. Only save a recurring transform once all known pairs pass exactly.

# Rebuilding after a rejected cached transform

A cached task program is only a first attempt, not evidence that its rule applies to the current instance. When its submission is rejected, retire the cached selector/operation and ask for a demonstration that can reveal a different rule. On each demo receipt, preserve exact input/output grids and compare changed cells, dimensions, palette roles, and unchanged regions across the complete ledger. State the hypothesis as a selector plus operation; do not issue serial demo requests without incorporating the previous pair.

Do not replace a task file with an identity or speculative placeholder while gathering evidence. That can make an unvalidated function look like a cache eligible for automatic submission on a later instance. Write only a credible transformation, run it against every exact demo pair, and retain it only after full equality checks. Generate the test candidate from that same verified transform.

This is especially important when examples appear diverse: one demo may reveal a localized transform, another may show propagation from a boundary, and another may alter a column or panel. Do not prematurely force them into a single guessed heuristic. Separate selector, operation, direction, and treatment of boundary markings, and request further evidence where those choices remain unresolved.

# Repeated rejection: reset the hypothesis, not just the code

In this stream instance, several local gap/line-completion guesses were submitted after successive incorrect verdicts. Each output was generated by code, but the proposed transforms were not exact-regressed against the accumulated demonstration pairs. The examples varied substantially in dimensions and visual structure, so superficial alignment between non-background cells was not enough to establish a shared operation. The eventual repeated attempts recycled variants of the same unvalidated interpretation instead of extracting a common selector and accounting for unchanged cells.

## Recovery lesson
- After rejection, explicitly retire the selector/operation that produced it. Do not continue with cosmetic changes to endpoints, gap length, or direction.
- Reconstruct the entire demo ledger before forming another candidate. Enumerate changed cells and relevant unchanged patterns; explain why each selected cell changes and why similar unselected cells do not.
- A local gap rule is only a candidate, not a task rule. Compare it against every orientation, distance, and layout shown in demos; broader outline completion or another structural operation may be relevant, but must be evidenced rather than guessed.
- Preserve exact fixtures and run full-grid equality regression on every pair before submission. Running a program only on the test input proves execution, not correctness.
- If complete fixtures were not preserved, acknowledge that the exact-demo gate was not satisfied. Use a remaining demo only to separate named alternatives, or select a materially distinct best-supported candidate rather than another minor variation.
- Remove unverified task files so a future recurrence does not treat a rejected guess as trusted cache.

This is a process postmortem, not a claim that this instance's transformation was solved.

# Session lesson: test immediate gap hypotheses across orientations

In this instance, demos shared a local rule across different grid sizes and palettes: recolor a background cell to 2 when it lies between matching non-background cells in a straight line. The demonstrated gaps were one-cell gaps; rules that filled every cell between any two markers were overbroad. The test included marker pairs with varying distances, so the distinction was consequential.

## Reusable inference and validation
- Compare exact input/output differences; note unchanged gaps, distances, and alignments, not merely a broad story such as “connect markers.”
- Test horizontal and vertical interpretations separately, then combine only if all demos show the same selector in both orientations.
- For each proposed rule, run the implementation over every accumulated full fixture. Small hand-written spot checks are not a substitute: one earlier check encoded an incorrect expected grid and failed, exposing the mistake.
- Keep the task program's `transform(grid)` as the source of the submitted grid; serialize its actual result.

## Caution
This session's candidate was not proven against all full fixtures before submission. The process lesson is to retain exact fixtures and regression-test them, not to treat the apparent one-cell gap rule as an established solution for future tasks.

# Review note: one-cell gap task and process failure

The task's prior linked lesson correctly warned that the visual rule involved filling only a one-cell background gap between matching marker cells in a straight horizontal or vertical line; longer-distance bridging was unsupported. Current demos independently confirmed this: in the horizontal patterns, a single background cell between marker endpoints changes to 2, while multi-cell gaps remain unchanged; vertical single gaps behave likewise.

The agent did not apply that note until after spending several demos, and generated unverified drafts without preserving all exact demo fixtures for regression. It then submitted a program output that failed to satisfy the earlier pairs. This is a workflow failure, not a reason to loosen the selector: consult matching task notes early, preserve fixtures losslessly as soon as each demo arrives, and explicitly compare exact changed cells and unchanged gaps before deciding whether another demo is needed.

Takeaway: same-task reference notes are useful hypothesis leads when a task ID recurs, but must be validated against the complete current instance. For future instances, verify the cached transform first as required, then run every current demo before submission; never let prior-instance notes replace current evidence.

# Long mixed demo stream: process lesson

In this session, eight examples were requested without maintaining a fixture ledger or running candidate transforms against the accumulated pairs. The examples visibly varied in palettes and spatial layouts; broad recoloring/identity conjectures were not sufficiently grounded. A first submission was incorrect, after which another unsupported recoloring was submitted despite the exhausted demo cap. Do not let a poorly managed evidence stream lead to more speculative submissions.

For future long Continual-ARC instances, capture every demo pair as it arrives, summarize changed coordinates/colors, and keep explicit competing selector-operation hypotheses. Run each candidate against every fixture; submit only if exact agreement is achieved. If demo requests are exhausted and no candidate passes, retire failed hypotheses and avoid presenting identity or a test-specific guess as a verified reusable rule. Keep the per-task cache absent unless a verified transform exists.

# Retrospective: mixed demos without an executable ledger

This task's eight demos varied widely in grid size, palette, separator structures, and the locations/types of changed regions. Despite that, the solving turns repeatedly requested more examples without recording complete fixtures or running a coherent hypothesis across the accumulated pairs. Several submissions were unsupported guesses (including broad recoloring, component-size rules, bounding-box filling, and identity); all were rejected. No transformation reproduced every demonstration, so the task program was correctly left absent at the terminal verdict.

Reusable lesson: as each demo arrives, capture its full input and output immediately in executable fixtures. Compute changed cells and run a candidate against all fixtures before requesting another demo or submitting. State what candidate alternatives the next demo is meant to discriminate. If no rule accounts for varied local changes, do not substitute a plausible test-only guess; preserve no speculative cache.

This is a process retrospective, not a proposed task rule: the received data in this record is insufficiently transcribed for a verified transform.

# Session review: serial demo requests without fixture analysis

In this Continual-ARC instance, seven demonstrations arrived, but the response after each one was another demo request. I did not build an executable ledger, compute pairwise changed cells, or test a shared selector-operation hypothesis. The examples were varied in grid size, palette, and localized edits; the central process failure was to treat acquisition as progress instead of analyzing the evidence already returned. The demo budget reached its cap without a supported transform or test output.

Reusable lesson: after every demo receipt, stop and analyze before taking the next action. Capture the full pair, determine the exact changed cells/regions and unchanged lookalikes, update candidate rules, and run any candidate over all accumulated fixtures. Request again only when a specific unresolved alternative has a discriminating feature that another example could reveal. Do not conclude the task is heterogeneous or unsolvable based only on visual diversity. Keep the task cache absent unless a transform reproduces all pairs exactly.

# Continual-ARC demo integration gate

Use for incremental ARC demonstrations, especially when pairs are large or vary in geometry, palette, or layout.

## Per-demo procedure
1. Treat every received pair as an analysis checkpoint. Compare it with all earlier pairs and record dimensions, changed cells, unchanged lookalikes, and color roles. Preserve exact fixtures whenever practical.
2. State the candidate as selector + operation + palette/placement mapping. Note what the latest pair confirms, contradicts, or leaves unresolved.
3. Before choosing an evaluator action, apply the candidate to the current test input and derive a prediction, or explicitly identify why the test has a new structural case.
4. Request another demo only after naming a plausible competing hypothesis and the observable feature in a future pair that would separate it. Avoid serial requests without integrating the previous pair; tool and skill reloads are not evidence progress.
5. Implement and run the transform against every complete fixture before submitting. Submit only its generated test grid. Do not preserve an unvalidated or test-specific placeholder as a recurring solution.

## Failure mode
A demo stream can be consumed through reflexive requests while leaving each returned example unexamined. This wastes budget and can conceal a simple invariant across examples. Make forward inferential progress on every turn between requests.

## Related skills
`continual-arc-solving` covers lifecycle and action protocol; `continual-arc-evidence-ledger` covers fixture fidelity; `continual-arc-demo-budgeting` covers request economics. These overlap with this integration workflow and should be considered for consolidation.

# Continual-ARC demo-loop discipline

Use alongside `continual-arc-solving` when demonstrations arrive incrementally, especially when examples vary in layout or the demo budget is large.

## Required per-demo checkpoint
1. Immediately after each demo, summarize its distinguishing input/output changes and compare them with all earlier pairs. Preserve exact fixtures whenever possible; do not rely on visual memory for large grids.
2. Update the candidate rule as separate selector, operation, palette, and placement hypotheses. Mark what the new example supports, contradicts, and leaves open.
3. Before another request, name a remaining alternative and a concrete feature in a hypothetical example that would discriminate it. If you have not analyzed the latest pair, do not spend another demo request.
4. Keep one evaluator action per turn. Tool calls are not evaluator progress: avoid cycles of reloading unchanged skills, repeating filesystem checks, or speculative edits when the next evidence action is already clear.
5. If exact fixtures were not captured, be candid that a candidate is not demo-verified. Do not create an identity or test-shaped placeholder in the recurring program library. Only persist a general transform after exact regression over all available pairs.

## Failure mode
A long instance can consume most of its demo budget through serial requests without incorporating each returned example. An unvalidated, bespoke candidate then risks replacing useful evidence-based work. Treat every received demo as a mandatory analysis gate before any next request or submission.

## Related skills
Use `continual-arc-solving` for lifecycle and action protocol, `continual-arc-evidence-ledger` for exact fixture management, and `continual-arc-demo-budgeting` for request economics. These overlap in demo-loop guidance; curator consolidation may be appropriate.

# Separator-edge inference: task-ea02ae1e review

A useful cross-demo candidate appeared in a mixed-orientation task: a full color-2 line separates an active panel; color 8 is added along one full panel boundary. The samples establish that output placement is sensitive to orientation and which side contains the non-background object. Across the horizontal-divider examples, the added line sits on an edge of the object-containing region (not on the divider); a vertical-divider sample adds a full-height color-8 line at the active region's outer edge. This suggests a reusable edge-marking family, but the exact edge-selection rule must still be verified against every pair before submission.

## Analysis recipe
1. Locate any full row/column of divider color and identify the bounded panel(s).
2. Identify background and salient object color from the region, not by assuming a fixed palette. Account for sparse object cells embedded in a large panel.
3. Record the exact changed output cells. Is the added 8-line adjacent to the divider or at the panel's far edge? Is it parallel to the divider?
4. Compare orientation and object-side across all demos. Treat 'nearest boundary' and 'farthest boundary' as competing hypotheses until discriminated.
5. Implement after the evidence supports a single rule; regress every exact pair, then generate test output from that transform. Do not create, repeatedly rewrite, or submit an unverified placeholder.

## Review lesson
This session repeatedly requested examples and made speculative program edits without capturing/regressing the exact fixtures. A later example clarified the geometry but did not retroactively validate those candidates. The correct recovery is to analyze the entire sequence as an evidence ledger and request another pair only if it distinguishes an explicitly stated remaining alternative. This note records the reasoning pattern, not a validated solution program for the task.

# Session review: integrating heterogeneous demos before action

In this instance, eight diverse pairs were requested with little integration of the returned evidence. The examples varied in dimensions, palettes, and layouts, yet a recurring relation was visible across the line-like cases: a uniform full-length color-2 guide was retained while the immediately adjacent field-line was recolored 8 (the guide itself was unchanged). The final 4x17 test has a short vertical 2 guide at column 14 beside a 0-pattern at column 13, with color 4 as background; the observed relation strongly suggests recoloring that adjacent column's background cells to 8 while preserving its 0 cell(s) and the 2 guide. This is a hypothesis, not confirmed by the incomplete fixture ledger in this run.

Process lessons: preserve every complete pair as an executable fixture on receipt; compare exact changed cells and unchanged lookalikes across all examples before requesting again. Treat each request as a question with a stated discriminator, not as forward progress by itself. The solver created an identity placeholder, attempted scratch checks without capturing the long demos, then emitted a speculative transform and ultimately submitted a hand-shaped fallback after the task program had been removed. Do not repeat this sequence: only submit a grid generated by the saved transform, and only retain a task program after exact regression on all captured demos. If the budget is exhausted without a validated rule, distinguish a best-supported unverified candidate from a verified solution and avoid persisting it.

# Continual-ARC evidence ledger and recovery

Use this class-level workflow whenever a task has multiple demo pairs, especially after a rejection or when examples vary in palette, orientation, or geometry.

## Maintain exact evidence
- Preserve each complete input/output grid with dimensions, palette, and arrival order. Build fixtures directly from received data rather than retyping selectively.
- Compare full grids, enumerate changed cells, and record important unchanged lookalikes. Separate selector (which cells/objects), operation (copy, extend, recolor, overlay), palette mapping, orientation, placement anchor, and boundary behavior.
- Check whether one abstract rule explains all pairs. Different layouts can be rotations or variants of one rule; do not force a surface-specific heuristic or assume task-id sameness is evidence by itself.

## Hypothesis and demo economics
1. State the leading candidate and a plausible alternative when uncertainty remains.
2. Before requesting a demo, identify what observable feature would distinguish those alternatives. If no likely example separates them, reconsider whether the request is useful.
3. After every received pair, integrate it, update the candidate, and run exact regression across every accumulated fixture before deciding the next action. Repeated requests without analysis are not progress.
4. After a wrong submission, retire that selector-operation hypothesis; do not make cosmetic palette, offset, phase, or endpoint tweaks absent new evidence.

## Program and submission gate
- Check the per-task cache first when an instance begins. Preserve exact demos and implement a general `transform(grid)` in the task-id file.
- Only call a transform demo-validated when every complete fixture matches exactly, including shape, changed and unchanged cells, and boundaries. Successful execution or valid payload shape is not semantic validation.
- Generate the test output by calling that same transform immediately before submission; never hand-edit the grid.
- If the budget forces a choice without a passing rule, regard the candidate as unverified, choose the strongest materially supported hypothesis, and do not persist speculative code as a reusable solution.
- Remove an unverified file created during the attempt so it is not mistaken for trusted cache on recurrence. Persist only a verified general solution after the verdict.

## Pitfalls
- Do not infer from one demo that a marker selects a particular direction, color, or motif placement; use cross-pair evidence and negative cases.
- Avoid using global frequency alone to assign every non-background color a role when multiple palettes or motifs coexist.
- Do not claim regression succeeded if a fixture is incomplete, malformed, or only spot-checked.
- Keep the evaluator action protocol distinct: exactly one allowed action per turn, with only the action JSON on the final line.

This umbrella complements `continual-arc-solving` (task lifecycle/action protocol), `continual-arc-demo-budgeting` (request economics), `continual-arc-instance-evidence` (fixture ledger), and `continual-arc-regression-discipline` (exact gate). They overlap substantially; curator consolidation may be warranted.

# Review lesson: integrate before issuing the next action

A multi-demo Continual-ARC session can satisfy the one-action JSON protocol while still making little inference progress: repeatedly requesting examples without preserving fixtures or analyzing the latest pair spends budget and defers the required selector/operation reasoning. After each receipt, first compare the exact changed cells and important unchanged cells against every prior demo and the test; state what uncertainty remains and whether the new pair discriminates hypotheses. Only then choose the next action. File existence checks, program invocations, and further skill-reference browsing do not count as demo integration. When complete fixtures are available, run the candidate on the entire accumulated set and require exact equality before submission. Do not describe a transform as validated when the pairs were not captured and checked.

# Session lesson: a lucky cached guess is not a reusable rule

In a multi-demo Continual-ARC instance, the initial cached transform was an unsupported motif-copy heuristic and was rejected. The workflow then drifted into repeated demo requests without integrating full fixtures, and later candidate programs were changed repeatedly without exact regression against every pair. Similar-looking motif families varied materially: horizontal and vertical line seeds, multicolor compact patterns, differing marker colors, and unrelated sparse geometry. Some local examples were made to fit, but no unified rule was demonstrated across all six examples.

Reusable lesson: after every returned pair, stop and update a complete evidence ledger before another action. Treat selector, encoded motif, operation, placement, palette, and orientation independently. Exact-check accumulated pairs; if they do not support a common transform, another request should have a named discriminator. Never leave an identity transform or speculative heuristic in the task cache, and never describe output as validated without full-grid equality.

# Continual-ARC evidence recovery

Use alongside `continual-arc-solving` when an answer is rejected, the demo budget is nearly exhausted, or cross-demo validation is incomplete.

## Recovery procedure
1. Retire the rejected selector/operation as a hypothesis; do not cosmetically vary its phase, offset, color, endpoints, or output dimensions.
2. Reconstruct and retain all received demo fixtures accurately. For each, record input/output dimensions and compare cellwise, including unchanged cells and absent-marker/default positions.
3. State candidate hypotheses explicitly as selector plus operation. Check all examples against one general rule; different-looking layout families are a reason to test for a shared abstraction, not to assume it.
4. After every new pair, run the candidate against every fixture and require exact nested-grid equality before considering a submission. A successful execution, shape check, or plausible output is not semantic validation.
5. If evidence remains ambiguous and demo calls remain, request only a pair expected to distinguish named alternatives.
6. When demos are exhausted without any exact-match candidate, stop cycling guesses. If the protocol still requires a submission, select the most evidence-supported materially distinct hypothesis and treat it as unverified. Do not save the speculative implementation into the recurring task library; leave the task file absent or preserve a prior verified version.
7. For a final action, obtain the grid by executing the current task transform on the exact test input immediately before serializing it. Do not submit stale output from an earlier code version.

## Pitfalls
- Do not turn a failed guessed output into a persistent task rule.
- Do not claim demo validation unless every complete pair was actually run and matched exactly.
- Keep the required one-action JSON protocol distinct from internal analysis; include only the evaluator action in the final reply.

See `continual-arc-solving` for lifecycle and library instructions, and `arc-demo-validation` for exact fixture comparison.

# Postmortem: repeated unvalidated gap-fill submissions

This instance showed why the demo gate must be operational, not merely stated. The agent guessed a one-cell gap rule, but its own demo assertions failed; it then discarded the task file, later recreated it with a `_demo_checks()` function that returned `True` without testing fixtures, and submitted a candidate repeatedly despite incorrect verdicts. It also used whole-span fills after failing to reconcile the examples. The task ended unsolved after exhausting all submissions.

## Durable workflow lessons
- A failed assertion is a hard stop: do not proceed to submission. Identify the first mismatch and revise only with evidence.
- Do not use comments, placeholder functions, or manually asserted snippets as claimed regression. Store full fixture pairs and execute exact nested-list comparisons.
- On a wrong verdict, retire the submitted rule. Before any further submission, write down a materially distinct candidate and which full demo outputs support it.
- Do not spend remaining attempts on variants that generate the same or nearly same output. If no candidate satisfies all demonstrations, uncertainty remains; say so internally and avoid claiming validation.
- Task-specific reference notes are hypotheses, not guaranteed truths for current data. This task's old one-cell-gap note was not enough to justify repeated submissions.

## Overlapping skills
This guidance overlaps with `continual-arc-solving`, `continual-arc-post-error-recovery`, `continual-arc-regression-discipline`, and `continual-arc-fixture-regression`; the umbrella skill should link here and curator consolidation may reduce duplication.

# Session review: demo-regression and action-generation breakdown

This instance exhibited repeated workflow failures: guesses were submitted without exact regression across all demos; speculative programs were created then removed; regression assertions were malformed and failed when run; and the final submission was hand-serialized rather than generated by the task transform. Earlier instruction demanded program output only, so the final action violated the task workflow even though its grid was syntactically valid.

Reusable lessons: preserve complete fixtures as each pair arrives; immediately execute exact input/output comparisons; treat any failed assertion as a hard stop; use remaining demo budget to discriminate rather than rebuilding untested candidates; and, if forced to submit without a fully validated rule, still implement/run the chosen candidate transform on the exact test input. Never claim verified status or persist speculative code. This note documents process failures, not a reusable puzzle transformation.

# Continual-ARC execution integrity

Use alongside `continual-arc-solving` for any Continual-ARC instance, especially after a wrong submission or when working under a tight action/time budget.

## Workflow
1. **Keep one evaluator action per turn.** The evaluator contract is strict; tools may be used internally, but the final response contains exactly one allowed JSON action.
2. **Execute before submitting.** Use the task-id program to generate the exact test output immediately before submission. Validate dimensions, row widths and palette from the generated result, then serialize it without hand edits. A grid copied from reasoning or partly assembled manually is not acceptable.
3. **Audit tool outcomes.** A successful file write or running program does not establish semantic correctness. Inspect failures: broken assertions, malformed fixtures, wrong import paths, or unexpected output indicate work remains. Fix the actual cause and rerun. Never treat a failed check as a pass.
4. **Capture demonstration fixtures faithfully.** Preserve dimensions and every cell. Run the candidate transform against every available input-output pair and require exact nested-grid equality. If fixture transcription is incomplete, do not claim validation.
5. **Budget evidence requests.** Before each request, identify competing hypotheses and the expected discriminating observation. Incorporate every returned pair and update the candidate. Do not spend repeated requests without doing analysis in between.
6. **Recover rigorously after rejection.** Retire the rejected selector and operation. Do not make cosmetic changes to the same unsupported rule. Use remaining demos to distinguish materially different explanations. If the user explicitly directs no further exploration due to a time/model budget, comply and make the best evidence-based choice from existing information.
7. **Persist only validated reusable code.** Save or replace the task program only when it exactly reproduces all accurately captured demos. If no candidate passes, do not turn a speculative test-specific output into a recurring library rule.

## Common traps
- Confusing valid JSON/grid shape with a correct transformation.
- Repeating demo requests without considering their cost or information value.
- Submitting manually edited output after a tool call failed or produced unexpected results.
- Leaving diagnostic assertions or unverified fixtures in the reusable program.

## Related guidance
For the standard task lifecycle, consult `continual-arc-solving`. For demo economics consult `continual-arc-demo-budgeting`; for post-rejection recovery consult `continual-arc-failure-recovery` and `continual-arc-evidence-recovery`. These existing skills overlap with this one; curator consolidation may be appropriate.

# Continual-ARC recovery after a wrong submission

Use whenever an attempt is marked incorrect and the instance remains active.

## Recovery steps
1. Treat the incorrect verdict as evidence that the submitted transformation failed. Do not tweak the same unsupported guess or replace it with an unrelated convenient palette/panel mapping.
2. Preserve a complete ledger of all demos: exact input and output dimensions, every row, colors, and orientations. Compare full grids cell-by-cell; note which regions change and which remain unchanged.
3. State a candidate as a selector plus an operation. The selector must explain both positive and negative cases, not just a few matching cells. Test panel and separator hypotheses against every example before accepting them.
4. If the rule is still uncertain and demo requests remain, ask for a pair designed to distinguish named alternatives. Each request costs points, so identify what uncertainty it resolves.
5. Implement the candidate in the task program and run exact full-grid equality checks against every received demo. A transform that merely executes or yields plausible output is not verified.
6. Only submit output actually generated by that program after it reproduces all demos. If no candidate meets the gate, do not falsely claim verification; use the most discriminating remaining evidence opportunity before any further submission.
7. After the instance ends, replace the task program only if it represents a transformation verified against all demos. Otherwise leave the prior file unchanged rather than saving a speculative mapping.

## Pitfalls
- Avoid palette substitution, guessed panel selection, fixed row slices, and hardcoded dimensions introduced only to match the current test.
- Do not keep adjusting a disproven hypothesis without new evidence.
- A session with several unsuccessful attempts is a reason to become stricter about evidence, not looser.

See `continual-arc-solving` for the per-turn JSON protocol and task-program lifecycle; see `arc-demo-validation` for detailed fixture and exact-equality practice.

# Demo-cap and terminal-recovery lesson

In a capped Continual-ARC puzzle, a request after the cap can be refused. Treat that as a protocol response, not as another pair, and immediately switch to analysis of the accumulated ledger. A rejected submission invalidates its rule hypothesis; do not alternate between a no-op/identity output and another unsupported hand-built grid.

When the evidence is insufficient, keep the distinction between (a) a program that happens to run and (b) a demo-validated transform. Do not save a placeholder as a reusable per-task program. With remaining attempts, use a materially different candidate only if it is grounded in all demonstrations; otherwise acknowledge internally that no supported hypothesis is available and avoid representing speculation as verified. In every case the evaluator still requires exactly one allowed action, and `finish` is unavailable until the instance is over.

This session’s attempts to extrapolate scattered motif/color propagation from multiple visibly distinct demos did not yield an exact validated rule. The reusable lesson is the cap/refusal handling and the prohibition against identity fallback—not any specific inferred grid operation.

# Sparse diagonal motif: avoid speculative checkerboard recovery

In this task family, examples with full-width color bands and examples with sparse diagonal traces both expanded into periodic textures, but their output periods and palettes differed. A test containing two diagonal traces colored 5 and 6 was not solved by either a 2-color checkerboard or by broad alternating diagonal bands; both attempts were rejected. The remaining demos included cycles with three or more colors and nontrivial phase offsets, so merely using the observed test colors was not justified.

After a wrong periodic-pattern submission:
- Retire the specific period, phase, and color mapping together; do not retry parity inversions or shifted versions without evidence.
- Compare diagonal displacement and motif geometry against every diagonal demo. Ask what colors are explicitly encoded and how unmarked cells map, rather than inferring this from color count alone.
- Require exact full-output equality on all demos. If the test-specific motif has no matching validated rule and demo budget is exhausted, do not create a speculative transform or claim it was validated.

This is an inference caution, not a reliable alternative solution algorithm; the task ended without a validated test rule.

# Mixed-demo recovery discipline: session lesson

A recurring task supplied multiple demonstrations with different visual structures (solid panels, rectangular color fields, sparse markers, and dense patterned regions). The attempted solutions repeatedly treated isolated cells as removable noise, then varied that same idea rather than establishing a selector against the examples. Several submissions were valid grids generated by a saved transform, but none reproduced the task; execution and payload shape were mistaken for evidence of semantic correctness.

## Reusable guardrails
- Start from exact input/output differences, not an intuitive test-grid cleanup rule. Record unchanged as well as changed cells.
- Separate candidate selector from operation: which cells/objects are selected, and what happens to them? Check both true and false cases across each demo.
- Do not skip exact demo verification. If fixtures are not runnable locally, encode them and assert complete grid equality before another submission; never imply this check was performed if it was not.
- After a wrong verdict, retire the rejected hypothesis. Repeated variants of singleton removal are not new hypotheses unless fresh evidence supports them.
- Every submission has real cost. Use remaining attempts only for a distinct rule supported by multiple demos; validate dimensions, palette, and payload, but do not confuse those checks with task correctness.
- Once the instance ends, leave no speculative recurring transform behind. Save only a rule that passes all demos, then perform the required finish action.

This is a process postmortem, not a task-specific transform.

# Payload validity versus semantic rejection

In a Continual-ARC recovery turn, inspect the evaluator's exact verdict before changing the rule. If it explicitly reports an invalid ARC grid, audit the final serialized payload independently: nonempty rectangular rows, equal row widths, integer cells in 0–9, and dimensions within limits. A syntactically valid JSON list can still have a malformed row. If the verdict only says incorrect, treat it as semantic rejection and retire the failed transformation rather than blaming serialization.

After a demo arrives, add the full exact pair to fixtures and rerun the current transform against every pair. Check both exact equality and payload shape: a valid-looking output is not evidence the inferred rule is correct. If the rule is still underdetermined, request another demo only when it distinguishes explicit competing hypotheses. Never submit until a program reproduces all available examples exactly.

# Rejected cached transforms: evidence-first recovery

A task-specific transform may exist before a new instance begins. The evaluator's procedure can require running it immediately, but successful execution only produces a candidate output; it does not establish that the transform fits this instance.

After an incorrect verdict:
- Retire the candidate rule. Do not preserve it by unsupported palette swaps, parity changes, or other cosmetic edits.
- Treat the task file as untrusted for this instance. Use all demos received to infer a replacement, and request additional pairs when they resolve a named ambiguity.
- Run exact full-grid comparisons against every demo before submitting. Do not mistake plausible output, a valid grid, or successful program execution for demo validation.
- Preserve an older file unless the replacement is verified; replace only with a demo-consistent transform after the instance is resolved.
- Keep evaluator messages to one allowed action JSON per turn, independently of internal analysis and tools.

This session illustrates why: a cached transform mapped coordinates to an invented 5/6 periodic fill; it was rejected. The first demo showed a blank upper area becomes a repeated row-color sequence (including colors absent from many source rows); a second showed a different sparse diagonal encoding expanded to a repeating 9/3 pattern. These are not sufficient to establish the test's precise expansion rule, so further discriminating evidence and exact validation are essential.

# Repeated guesses after wrong verdicts

This session showed a failure mode: after an unsupported checkerboard submission was marked wrong, subsequent submissions changed only phase/orientation and then guessed diagonal bands at a five-cell spacing. Those changes were not supported by a discriminating demo and consumed attempts without improving the evidence base.

After a wrong verdict, retire the whole rule family, not just the exact grid phase. For sparse diagonal motifs, distinguish the encoded dimension (diagonal offset, color cycle, stroke spacing, or wraparound) from the expansion operation before producing a new grid. Do not infer a period just because two traces are separated by that many cells. When demos are exhausted, avoid serial cosmetic variants; if submission is mandatory, form one materially different hypothesis tied to the demonstrated mappings and produce its output via the task program.

# Divergent demonstration families under one task ID

A stream task can present demonstrations whose source layouts differ sharply: horizontal color bands, sparse diagonals, and tiny triangular motifs. Do not assume they all arise from one simple fill rule merely because they share an instance ID. Track each input motif family and its output relationship explicitly, then demand one coherent transform that accounts for all pairs. A rule matching one family but failing others is not validated.

After a wrong answer, retire the complete hypothesis family. In particular, changing checkerboard phase, swapping colors, or guessing a new diagonal period is not meaningful recovery without new evidence. If demos are exhausted, recognize that uncertainty remains; any required guess should be a distinct hypothesis grounded in observed mappings, not an asserted verified program.

# Retrospective: repeated guesses after demo exhaustion

This instance exhausted its demo budget and accumulated several rejected submissions. The main failure was failing to convert the demos into a complete executable fixture ledger, then cycling among panel overlap, blank-panel extraction, and whole-panel recoloring guesses. These candidates were often submitted without exact regression against every pair, and one action manually serialized a grid rather than consistently submitting the transform's returned output.

## Reusable lessons
- After a rejection, retire the specific rule and inspect its counterexample; do not resubmit it or a cosmetic variant.
- As soon as each demo arrives, preserve full input/output grids and run a single harness over all fixtures. If fixtures were not captured, reconstruct before forming another candidate.
- Separate questions: which panel supplies output geometry, how marks are selected, and how colors map. A solid divider alone does not establish that output is the intersection, union, or recoloring of a panel.
- After demos are exhausted, spend each remaining submission only on a distinct, explicit hypothesis supported by observations. If no useful alternate exists, avoid repeated near-identical guesses.
- Always call the task transform on the exact test input and submit precisely that program output; do not hand-compose a payload that bypasses the required program.
- Only keep a recurring task program if it exactly reproduces all available demos. Remove speculative files when no candidate passed.

# Continual-ARC fixture regression discipline

Use when Continual-ARC examples are lengthy, repeated demo requests are being considered, or a submission has been rejected.

## Workflow
1. Preserve every demo input and expected output as complete executable fixtures as soon as it arrives, including dimensions and all rows. Avoid repeatedly transcribing long grids into ad-hoc shell commands.
2. Express the hypothesis as an explicit selector plus operation. Check positive and negative cells, output shape, palette mapping, and default/absent-marker behavior separately.
3. After each new demo, run the task transform across the entire accumulated fixture set and compare nested lists exactly. A successful run on only the current test grid is not validation.
4. On mismatch, inspect the first differing cell and output shape; retire the unsupported hypothesis rather than tweaking a sampling offset, phase, palette, or orientation without discriminating evidence.
5. Request another demo only after naming unresolved alternatives and what feature of the next example would distinguish them.
6. Submit only output generated by the same transform that passes every fixture. If evidence cannot be faithfully represented or no candidate passes, do not claim verification or overwrite the recurring task program with a speculative rule.

## Lattice-specific checks
For tiled grids with sparse marks on separator lines, establish tile pitch, separator coordinates, marker coordinate-to-output mapping, and output dimensions from all examples. Test unmarked/default output cells as carefully as colored marks; a single sampling offset that matches one layout may be wrong across varying orientations or tile sizes.

## Pitfalls
- Repeated requests without an executable fixture ledger waste demo budget and invite visual-memory errors.
- Test-only execution, plausible appearance, and shape validation do not establish demo consistency.
- Do not patch the program into increasingly ad-hoc row/column phases after a wrong answer.

See `references/lattice-fixture-checklist.md` for a compact per-demo record template.

# Retrospective: lattice extraction failed under budget pressure

This instance received eight large demonstrations across horizontal/vertical and mixed marker-lattice layouts. The output was a compact grid sampled from colored intersections, but I failed to faithfully record examples as executable fixtures, failed to derive the separator coordinates/output dimensions, and repeatedly made unsupported extraction attempts. I briefly wrote unvalidated program candidates and even submitted a fabricated small grid after exhausting demos. Those are failures, not a reusable algorithm.

## Carry-forward lessons
- A cached task file must be run unchanged on the test input before any other task action; writing a new file does not satisfy this first-trial requirement.
- Preserve all demos exactly in fixtures and use their outputs to infer the lattice pitch, which intersection coordinates encode cells, how blank crossings are represented, and compact dimensions. Validate all pairs after each implementation.
- Do not infer test output solely from visual marker pattern or construct a plausible placeholder. Submit only the output of a transform that passes the full demo suite.
- With all demo requests exhausted and no supported rule, any remaining submission is explicitly a best-effort guess, not validated; do not pretend it came from a verified program.

This note records process errors and must not be used as an extraction heuristic.

# Hollow-frame selector discipline

Use this class-level guidance when grids contain hollow rectangular outlines and only some interiors may be recolored.

1. Identify candidate frames using the exact geometric definition supported by demos. Check the full boundary and verify that the interior is initially background.
2. Record each candidate's interior height, width, area, outline color, and output treatment. Do not assume all candidate frames receive the same treatment.
3. Infer a selector from comparisons across demos: possible properties include square-vs-rectangular interiors, size, parity, palette, or spatial relation. A single observed frame is insufficient to establish that a property is causal.
4. Encode the frame predicate and selector separately in `transform(grid)`. Avoid broad filling every empty rectangle; equally, do not narrow to squares or another special case unless the examples distinguish that condition.
5. Exact-check the entire output against every available demo before submitting. Preserve all outlines and unrelated cells.

## Pitfall: plausible but unvalidated narrowing

In one task, a demo showed a 3x3 colored interior inside a square outline, while a distinct rectangular frame stayed unchanged. A square-interior selector initially looked sensible and produced a plausible test output, but it had not been verified by a second example; the correct next move was to request another demonstration rather than submit. This is a reminder that one demonstration can suggest geometry without uniquely determining the rule. The task instance did not reach a verdict, so do not treat square-only selection or a fixed fill color as established reusable rules.

## Action protocol

In Continual-ARC, still obey the task's one-action-per-turn JSON protocol. Request further demos when the selector remains ambiguous; submit only the output produced by the checked task program. Refer to `references/frame-selector-and-action-discipline.md` for this session's concise evidence ledger and failure mode.

Session evidence: One received example showed a rectangular outline with an empty 1x3 interior unchanged, and a 3x3 interior filled with color 4. These observations do not establish that square-ness is the selector, nor that 4 is universally the fill color. The test contained more than one candidate shape, so a square-only implementation was an unsupported narrowing, not a demo-validated rule. Proper action was to request a second demo to distinguish candidate selectors, and avoid submitting a speculative program output. The session's attempted pattern match also demonstrated why candidate geometry should be extracted and checked systematically rather than inferred from visual proximity alone.

# Continual-ARC inference discipline

Use this class-level supplement when a recurring lattice/panel task is ambiguous, when demos vary in structure, or after any incorrect submission.

## Procedure
1. Maintain a complete, faithful ledger of each demo pair. Preserve dimensions, all rows, and exact integer values; prefer executable fixtures over mental summaries.
2. State each hypothesis as a **selector plus operation**: which features/cells are selected, and what transformation is applied. Explicitly check positive and negative cases across all examples.
3. Separate structural questions: output dimensions, panel or separator selection, cell correspondence, palette mapping, and treatment of unmarked/default cells. Evidence for one does not establish the others.
4. After a wrong verdict, retire the failed selector/operation. Do not cycle through nearby sampling offsets, constants, phases, or guessed dimensions without new evidence.
5. Before submission, run the exact task transform on every captured demo and compare complete outputs. Require exact dimensions and cellwise equality; execution success, plausible appearance, and shape validation are not semantic validation.
6. Generate the test answer by calling that same transform. Validate rectangular, nonempty dimensions and palette range before serializing the action.
7. Once demos are exhausted, only use remaining attempts for a materially distinct, evidence-supported hypothesis. If none is supported, do not present an arbitrary placeholder as a solution; never label an unverified program as demo-verified or save it as a recurring rule.

## Common pitfalls
- Guessing output shape from test dimensions without establishing the relation from demos.
- Sampling divider intersections without proving which lines and offsets map to output cells.
- Treating all demos of one task ID as one visual family without checking that a coherent invariant explains them.
- Replacing a failed transform with constant grids or hand-picked grids merely because the action protocol requires one JSON object.
- Writing a task file before it implements a credible general rule; task-specific hardcoding of the current test defeats recurrence.

## References
See `references/exhausted-demo-session.md` for a cautionary session note on divergent lattice examples and the cost of unvalidated repeated submissions.

# Session-specific caution: complex lattice demos

This instance presented eight structurally varied periodic grids with compact outputs, but no complete demo fixtures were encoded or tested against the proposed transforms. Several guesses then used unsupported output dimensions, divider sampling, constant fills, and empty output after failed line detection. Each submission was wrong; later guesses did not constitute new evidence.

Reusable lesson: implement a general transform only after identifying its coordinate mapping from full examples. The demos' repeated look did not itself establish output width, output height, or whether values came from tile interiors, divider lines, or intersections. A failed grid detector should trigger a corrected candidate or another evidence request when available—not an empty grid. After cap exhaustion, a best-effort action may be unavoidable, but arbitrary constants and repeated variants have poor evidential basis. Keep task files only for transforms validated against every fixture.

# Heuristic drift after repeated rejections

Repeated ARC submission failures are a signal to stop making visually plausible edits and return to evidence.

- Keep complete, cumulative input/output fixtures from every demo request, including prior pairs and all rows.
- For each candidate, state a precise selector and operation before implementation. Identify cells that should change and similarly situated cells that should not.
- Run exact dimension and cell equality against every fixture after every rule change. A successful run, plausible-looking output, or check against only the latest demo/test is not validation.
- Retire a rejected rule rather than varying its radius, bounding box, direction, parity, or palette without new evidence.
- When demos are exhausted, submit only a materially distinct candidate supported across the fixture set; do not treat protocol pressure as evidence for a fallback guess. Persist only transforms that pass the full demo gate.

This instance's repeated unvalidated guesses (bounding-box completion, local dilation, and related color propagation) generated four rejected submissions and did not establish a common rule across the increasingly varied examples. The usable lesson is the cumulative exact-regression gate above, not any guessed transform.

# Serial demo request discipline

In an active Continual-ARC instance, incorporate each returned pair before asking for another. Preserve exact input/output grids and compare the new pair against every prior example. State which unresolved rule distinction another demo would answer; then update the transform candidate and run exact comparisons against the accumulated examples whenever possible. Avoid issuing repeated requests without analysis: demo requests consume score and do not replace hypothesis evaluation. If a demo disproves the candidate, retire it rather than layering speculative tweaks onto it.

# Continual-ARC instance evidence ledger

Use during multi-turn ARC instances where demos arrive incrementally, especially when grids are large or a task ID has historical notes.

## Evidence workflow
1. On every demo receipt, preserve the complete input and output grids, dimensions, and palette as current-instance fixtures. Keep all earlier fixtures; never rely on visual memory or a previous conversation's description.
2. Compute exact changed cells and record unchanged lookalike structures. Describe candidates as selector plus operation (and palette mapping when relevant); distinguish selector uncertainty from operation uncertainty.
3. Before another demo request, test the candidate against every accumulated pair by full grid equality. If it fails, identify mismatching cells and retire/refine only when evidence supports a distinct candidate. Request another demo only to discriminate named alternatives.
4. Submit only a grid produced by a task program that exactly reproduces all available demos. Successful invocation or plausible output is not semantic validation.
5. A recurring task ID or library retrospective may suggest pitfalls, but cannot replace checking the current cached program first or validating fresh demos. Verify current filesystem state and transcript evidence.
6. Save/replace the per-task program only when it represents a general rule validated on every available pair. Do not persist guesses or identity fallbacks as verified solutions.

## Pitfalls
- Repeatedly spending demo budget without integrating each pair leaves less opportunity while producing no stronger evidence.
- Prior session summaries can be incomplete or describe another instance; use them to avoid known mistakes, not invent current outputs.
- Do not claim exact validation unless complete fixtures were actually executed and compared.

## Related skills
Use `continual-arc-solving` for action protocol and task-program lifecycle, `continual-arc-regression-discipline` for exact accumulated-pair checks, and `continual-arc-demo-budgeting` for cost-aware selection. These skills overlap in evidence management; curator consolidation may be useful.

# Analyze before the next action

This instance illustrates demo-request drift: successive examples arrived, but the solver kept requesting another without incorporating evidence or updating a candidate. On receiving a demo, pause before choosing the next evaluator action. Record changes/unchanged lookalikes, update the accumulated evidence and competing selector-operation hypotheses, and assess whether the current set supports a transform. Request again only if a specific unresolved alternative exists and a plausible new pair could separate it. Do not treat requesting evidence as progress by itself; analysis and exact regression across fixtures are required after each receipt.

# Program invocation and post-success checks

During this Continual-ARC turn, an attempted cached-program invocation passed the textual placeholder `'[]'` rather than the actual test grid object. The transform consequently received malformed input and raised an indexing error; a later invocation using the real nested list produced the intended output. This illustrates a general invocation hazard: successful shell execution or plausible-looking output does not prove that the function received the exact fixture. Embed the grid as a proper Python list literal or JSON-decode it, and check expected height/width before running.

After the evaluator confirms a submission is correct and requests a library save, retain or write the general transform that reproduced the demos. A smoke test on a tiny unrelated grid only verifies importability/basic execution, not demo equivalence. When complete fixtures are available, run exact equality checks over all demo pairs before claiming the saved program reproduces them.

# Session note: integrate demos before asking again

In a recurring-motif task, the cached program was tried first and rejected. Several demos then arrived with different seed orientations and color roles. The solver repeatedly requested another example while failing to maintain a complete fixture ledger or run a cross-demo exact check after each receipt. It also rewrote the cached transform based on partial patterns without verifying every pair; the eventual test proposal remained unsupported. This is a workflow failure, not evidence for a particular motif rule.

Reusable recovery lessons:
- On each demo receipt, immediately capture complete input/output fixtures and report exact grid dimensions and changed coordinates.
- Distinguish seed-orientation/template uncertainty from selector uncertainty (which marks trigger copying) and operation uncertainty (how the template maps to output). Do not infer a marker merely from frequency if seed cells contaminate the counts.
- Run the current candidate over every fixture right away; if it fails, retain mismatch coordinates and explicitly retire/refine the rule before another request.
- Use a demo request only when a named pair of hypotheses makes different predictions on a likely new example.
- Never replace the task cache with a speculative rule. After an incorrect attempt, leave it absent unless a general transform passes all complete pairs.

This note records the failed workflow only; no task transformation from that instance was validated.

# Session lesson: motion hypotheses and malformed grids

This instance exposed two separable failure modes. Several demos supported a one-row downward translation, but the accumulated examples also included an unchanged pattern. Treating the shift as a universal rule therefore lacked a demonstrated condition; use boundary-touching and unchanged demos to distinguish unconditional translation from gated movement. Compare complete rows/cells across every pair, not just the visible object.

The test transcription also contained rows with 24 cells in a stated 25-column grid. This was detectable with a simple per-row width assertion before submission. An invalid ARC payload rejection may be caused by malformed serialization independently of semantic correctness. Validate input fixture dimensions and each row width, then validate output dimensions, row widths, palette, and values before creating the action JSON.

Practical guard:
```python
assert len(grid) == stated_height
assert all(len(row) == stated_width for row in grid)
out = transform(grid)
assert len(out) == stated_output_height
assert all(len(row) == stated_output_width for row in out)
assert all(0 <= value <= 9 for row in out for value in row)
```

Do not call a transform demo-verified unless full-grid equality has actually been checked on every received pair. If malformed output is rejected, repair fixture shape and rerun before changing the inferred transformation.

# Review: recurrent task reference and trustworthy regression fixtures

## What happened
For task `task-871ad6f0`, the first pair showed a hollow rectangular outline and a lone color-2 cell immediately outside its lower-right corner. A second pair, with a different background and marker palette, showed color 2 filling one-cell gaps between matching marker cells horizontally and vertically, while the original marker cells remained intact. The test likewise had several one-cell gaps, and a one-gap-only extension was a plausible candidate. The existing library already contained a review of this exact task ID describing this rule. That reference was consulted only after the initial demo request, so it did not inform demo budgeting.

A speculative transform was then written before the complete first demo had been reliably translated into a regression fixture. The hand-coded expected output for demo 1 was wrong: it assumed the lower-right cell of the outline should change, rather than faithfully encoding the actual demonstrated output. The run failed an assertion on demo 2 too. This is not evidence that the general rule failed; it is evidence the candidate/fixtures were not validated. The speculative file was removed, and no test answer was submitted.

## Durable workflow lesson
- Look for task-ID-specific references at instance start, alongside the mandated cached-program check. Such notes are hypothesis leads that may save demo cost, not substitutes for this instance's exact demos.
- Transcribe full input/output grids before deriving a transform. Keep fixtures immutable and use exact equality; do not infer a fixture from a prose summary or visual impression.
- For a one-cell-gap candidate, test all directions and negative cases: matching non-background endpoints with exactly one background cell between them; longer gaps stay unchanged; endpoints and unrelated cells remain unchanged. Handle simultaneous candidates based on the original input, not cascading updates.
- A regression assertion failure must stop the workflow. Inspect computed-versus-expected mismatches, first determining whether the fixture was transcribed correctly, then whether the rule is wrong. Do not submit, overwrite a known-good program, or describe the transform as demo-verified until every complete pair passes.
- If prior task notes and current evidence are insufficient or inconsistent, request a discriminating demo rather than manufacturing an expected output.

This instance did not reach a verdict, so the one-gap hypothesis remains a useful candidate, not a verified answer for this instance.

# Continual-ARC iterative inference under failed hypotheses

Use when a candidate has been rejected, or when newly received demonstrations appear to use different separator orientations or panel layouts.

## Recovery workflow
1. Retire the exact rejected rule. Do not patch it by swapping colors, complementing a selector, or changing a panel slice unless new evidence discriminates that variant.
2. Maintain a faithful ledger of every input/output demo, with dimensions and all rows. Record selector candidates and their exact predicted full output per pair.
3. Treat layout/orientation as a hypothesis, not as a license for independent special cases. Determine whether demos are consistent with one abstract operation under rotation, reflection, or panel extraction; if not established, request another pair that discriminates plausible rule families.
4. Do not overwrite a verified program with an unverified guess. A candidate becomes eligible for submission only after it reproduces every available demo exactly, including output dimensions, palette, and every cell.
5. Verify fixtures themselves: compare each entered expected grid against the transcript, especially dimensions and final rows. A malformed or mismatched fixture can falsely validate a hypothesis.
6. Generate the test answer by running the verified transform, and submit exactly that result. Inspect row lengths and expected panel/canvas geometry before submission.
7. Save a new recurring-task transform only after it passes the exact demo gate; otherwise preserve the previous known-good file.

## Pitfalls
- A code path that executes or produces plausible output is not evidence of demo agreement.
- “Complement,” “intersection,” or “overlay” are not selectors until they explain every positive and negative cell in all examples.
- Never decide the operation by fitting only one demo after a wrong answer; distinguish alternatives with the remaining demo budget.
- Keep the required one-action JSON protocol separate from internal analysis; the final line must be exactly one allowed action.

## Related skills
Use `continual-arc-solving` for the standard instance lifecycle and `arc-demo-validation` for cellwise fixture comparison.

# Divider and panel hypothesis checks

Use these checks when demos contain grids split by a solid line or differently oriented layouts.

1. Transcribe exact input and output dimensions and rows from every demo before comparing rules. Retain fixtures; do not trust an incomplete or malformed local transcription.
2. Locate candidate separators by checking all rows and all columns, but distinguish interior lines from uniform edge rows/columns. Confirm the candidate actually separates the demonstrated regions and yields the observed output canvas dimensions.
3. For each candidate interpretation, compute exact cellwise output on every demo. Record changed/unchanged cells and compare palette mappings; do not infer an operation from visual plausibility or one matching demo.
4. When a hypothesis fails, retire it. Do not repeatedly change panel slices, background rules, or complements without evidence that discriminates the new variant.
5. If available demos permit multiple selectors, request a pair designed to distinguish them. Submit only after the task program exactly reproduces all demos and generates the test output.

In particular, a task may reuse a separator-like visual cue across examples without sharing the same panel operation. Check for independently demonstrated abstract invariance before applying horizontal/vertical special cases.

# Mixed-layout hypothesis discipline

A large set of visually similar divider examples does not prove that all demos belong to one separator/panel transformation family. In particular, do not force a divider-based rule onto an example whose output geometry, palette, or mark placement does not align with that hypothesis.

For each candidate, preserve a per-demo ledger and generate the exact full output. Compare all cells and dimensions. Treat equal-color overlay, union, intersection, complement, and recoloring as distinct hypotheses; reject each unless its selector explains both changed and unchanged cells across all examples. Sparse or nearly empty outputs are still evidence: they may reveal that only a specific motif or relation is selected, not that the chosen panel mapping is correct.

After a wrong submission, retire the failed selector. Before another submission, obtain discriminating evidence where available and run a single transform across all captured pairs. Do not accept code that merely runs or matches a partial visual impression.

Fixture transcription is part of verification. Preserve every row exactly, count dimensions, and compare generated output against the transcript's complete expected grid. Never infer task rule from a fixture you have not checked for transcription fidelity.

# Mixed demo families and rejected fallback: session lesson

In one Continual-ARC instance, multiple early demo pairs showed sparse or patterned marks and outputs recoloring selected cells to 2, but later pairs had distinctly different layouts and selectors. The sequence was treated as one presumed class of transformation without ever establishing an exact cross-demo rule. Multiple speculative candidate programs were created and removed; importantly, none was regression-tested against all complete pairs, and the final submission was an unchanged copy of the test grid. That submission was rejected.

## Reusable recovery lesson
- A repeated task ID is not evidence that every demo pair shares one surface-level transformation. Compare full geometry and changes; state explicitly whether a single abstract rule fits all pairs or whether the evidence implies heterogeneous task families.
- Do not reach for identity output simply because a candidate is hard to infer. Identity is a hypothesis and needs evidence like any other rule.
- After a rejection, retire the exact submitted hypothesis, then use the remaining budget on an informative demo or evidence-led inference. Do not make another submission until the transform predicts every received pair exactly.
- Keep unverified candidates out of the recurring program cache; persist only demo-validated general transforms.

# Repeated rejection and fixture validation

When an inference session accumulates several wrong submissions, stop trying small changes to the same hypothesis. Maintain an exact ledger of all demos and compare complete outputs, including dimensions and every cell. Validate fixture transcription (row count and row widths) before treating a computed match as evidence.

A submission candidate must explain both selected and unselected cells across every demo. Treat separator orientation, panel projection, overlap/union, and palette mapping as separate claims. A failed verdict invalidates the current selector; revise only when fresh evidence supports a materially different rule. With demos exhausted, distinguish a best-effort guess from a verified rule and avoid overwriting a reusable program unless it passes every demo.

Keep the strict Continual-ARC one-action JSON response protocol throughout. The submitted grid must be generated by the task program.

# ARC motif-copy inference

Use when grids contain a compact multicolor motif plus sparse markers and outputs may replicate, translate, rotate, or stamp that motif.

## Workflow
1. Establish background, source motif, marker set, and irrelevant cells using structure: components, bounding boxes, adjacency, and repetitions. Do not infer color roles from global frequency alone; marker colors may also occur in the motif.
2. State the full candidate: source selector, marker selector, orientation, marker-to-motif anchor offset, whether markers remain or are overwritten, collision behavior, clipping, and handling of existing non-background cells.
3. Compare all demos for a shared abstract operation while independently checking palette, dimensions, motif geometry, marker placement, and output changes. Varying layouts do not justify forcing a single untested geometry or abandoning a shared relational rule.
4. Preserve every complete fixture verbatim. After each new pair, run the candidate on every accumulated input and require exact nested-grid equality. Diagnose mismatches; execution or visual plausibility is not validation.
5. Before requesting another demo, name unresolved selector/anchor/overlay alternatives and the observation expected to distinguish them. Spend requests only when informative.
6. Generate submission output by executing the same transform that passed the full fixture suite. If no candidate passes, treat it as unverified and do not persist it as a trusted recurring-task cache.

## Pitfalls
- Most-frequent or rarest non-background color heuristics can misidentify the locator when motif colors and markers overlap.
- Center, corner, or marker-cell alignment is a hypothesis to test, not a default rule.
- A test-only successful run does not prove semantic correctness; exact checks must include every demo and untouched cells.
- Keep one allowed JSON action per Continual-ARC turn; after a correct verdict persist the demo-verified program and finish.

## Related skills
`continual-arc-solving` covers lifecycle and protocol; `continual-arc-evidence-ledger` and `continual-arc-regression-discipline` cover evidence capture and exact checking. These class-level skills overlap in evidence-gating and demo economics; consolidation may be useful.
